intro: Pan-Africanism is the idea that people of African descent share a history and an interest, and later that African states should unite. Its roots lie in the diaspora traced at the end of Pre-Colonial Africa; it was carried into the colonies by students and activists, met the nationalism growing inside Africa between the wars, and produced the Organisation of African Unity in 1963. This module also teaches source criticism through a famous document that turns out to be a modern fake.
outcomes: Trace Pan-Africanism from 1893 to 1963, and weigh the record on Garvey.
Describe interwar nationalism inside Africa, from the NCBWA to the Wafd and the Ethiopian crisis of 1935.
Explain why Manchester 1945 is called a turning point.
Compare the Casablanca and Monrovia groups, and say what the OAU Charter does and does not say about borders.
Apply four authenticity tests to a famous document and explain why the Willie Lynch letter fails them.

lessons.title: Roots, Garvey and the first Congresses

blocks.x: Pan-Africanism began outside the continent and was carried back by students and activists. It was never one programme: it ranged from cultural pride to continental government. {{lib}}
Roots
Nineteenth-century thinkers such as Edward Wilmot Blyden and Alexander Crummell, Ethiopianism in African churches, and the 1896 victory at Adwa all fed the idea. {{lib}}

In 1900 Henry Sylvester Williams, a Trinidadian lawyer, convened the Pan-African Conference in London. {{lib}} The date is conventional: one historian dates pan-Africanism to 1893, with a week-long meeting in Chicago, followed by Atlanta in 1895 and Williams's African Association in 1897. {{gha-ix}}
The movement was coined and nurtured mostly by diaspora intellectuals in the nineteenth century. {{gha-ix}}
Garvey
Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association, from 1914, used the slogan Africa for the Africans and ran the Black Star Line. {{lib}}

Garvey's own membership claims rose each year: 2 million by 1919, 4 million by 1920 and 6 million with 900 branches by 1923. They are self-reported and cannot be verified, and the editor of his papers says they were likely exaggerated. About 25,000 people filled Madison Square Garden on 01/08/1920. {{gv-auto}} {{gv-intro}}

The slogan did not mean self-rule by existing African peoples. In an open letter of 18/04/1922 he meant that Black people from across the world should build a nation in Africa, with diaspora settlers working in partnership with Africans. {{gv-afr}}

His Declaration of the Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World was adopted at the 1920 convention. It protests the partition of Africa, rejects taxation without representation, and demands Africa for the Africans at home and abroad. {{gv-decl}}

blocks.title: The record that critics such as Du Bois used
head: Fact
What the primary source or editor shows
rows: Meeting with the Ku Klux Klan
On 25/06/1922 in Atlanta he met the Klan's acting leader, and in a speech of 09/07/1922 said the UNIA and the Klan wanted the same thing {{gv-klan}}
On 13/02/1922 he welcomed a Mississippi senator's resolution urging the US to find an African home for Black Americans {{gv-sen}}
Convicted for selling stock after the line was insolvent; supporters called it a frame-up and the editor says it was badly run; deported in 1927 {{gv-intro}}
In 1924 Liberia, under pressure from European governments, refused the UNIA a settlement {{gv-lib}}

blocks.x: Du Bois published a critical article, Back to Africa, in the Century magazine in February 1923. Garvey's reply is polemic, so treat it as a partisan witness. {{gv-dubois}} {{gv-intro}}
Garvey died on 10/06/1940 in London and was reburied in Jamaica in 1964. He never entered an African country, yet Nkrumah said his writings fired his enthusiasm. {{gv-intro}}

So Pan-African organising was sparse before the First World War and regular only in the 1920s (our reading of the dates).

blocks.q: A poster says 'Pan-Africanism was born at the founding of the OAU in 1963.' Where did it actually begin?
o: In the Atlantic world, in the 1890s and 1900, among diaspora intellectuals
blocks.w: It was coined and nurtured mostly in the diaspora. {{gha-ix}}

blocks.q: A biography says Garvey led 6 million members. How should you report the figure?
o: As Garvey's own claim for 1923, unverifiable and likely exaggerated

i: Pan-Africanism began in the Atlantic world, conventionally in 1900. {{gha-ix}}
Garvey's numbers are his own claims; his critics had grounds. {{gv-intro}}
The Congresses of 1919 to 1927 asked for rights more than independence.

lessons.title: Nationalism inside Africa between the wars

blocks.x: Pan-Africanism from outside met nationalism growing inside Africa. Colonialism turned racial distinctions into class divisions and created a literate elite excluded from partnership, which led it into opposition. {{gha-vii-ch19}}
Nationalism was not only urban and elite: protest migrations, deposed chiefs and cocoa hold-ups belong to it too. {{gha-vii-ch22}}
West Africa: the NCBWA and its limits

The National Congress of British West Africa held its first conference in Accra in 03/1920, and its 1920 delegation to London was rejected. Later sessions met at Freetown (1923), Bathurst (1925 to 1926) and Lagos (1930). {{gha-vii-ch25}}

Garvey's weight is debated. One reading says Casely Hayford used the impetus of Garveyism to found the Congress; another credits Casely Hayford and Akiwande Savage and treats Garvey as a secondary influence. {{gha-vii-ch29}} {{gha-vii-ch25}} [CONTESTED]

The Congress pushed the elective-seat constitutions of Nigeria (1923), Sierra Leone (1924) and the Gold Coast (1925), but those seats 'anaesthetised' it, and its leaders were co-operationist. {{gha-vii-ch25}}

Other groups followed: the Gold Coast Youth Conference (1929), the Nigerian Youth Movement (1934) and the West African Students' Union. Unions were illegal until 1932 to 1941 in British territories and 1937 in French. {{gha-vii-ch25}}

The Negro World reached about 200,000 circulation and was banned in Nyasaland by 1922, and African students in the United States, among them Azikiwe from 1925 and Nkrumah from 1935, carried ideas home. {{gha-vii-ch29}}
Egypt, Sudan and Somaliland

Egypt's Wafd was formed in 11/1918, and Zaghlul's arrest on 08/03/1919 sparked a revolution across classes and faiths. Independence was declared on 28/02/1922 with four reserved points (communications, defence, minorities, Sudan), and the 1936 treaty legalised the British occupation. {{gha-vii-ne}}

In Sudan, the White Flag League (1924) and the Khartoum military revolt (11/1924) were followed by neo-Mahdism. In Somaliland, riots at Burao over western education (1922) preceded the Somali National League (1935). {{gha-vii-ne}}
Culture: Negritude and the press

Negritude had its manifesto in Legitime Defense by Martinican students, with Cesaire, Senghor and Damas as its midwives. {{gha-vii-ch21}} Egypt's press grew from 169 papers (1898) to 282 (1913). {{gha-vii-ch21}}
1935: Ethiopia, and Liberia's crisis

The Walwal incident was on 05/12/1934, and Italy invaded Ethiopia on 03/10/1935 without a declaration of war. The League voted 50 to 1 on 09/10/1935 but imposed no oil sanctions, and Italian troops entered Addis Ababa on 06/05/1936. {{gha-vii-ch28}}
The invasion stirred the diaspora. The International African Friends of Abyssinia formed in 08/1935 with Kenyatta as secretary. {{gha-vii-ch28}}
In Liberia, the Christy commission (08/09/1930) found forced recruitment of labour for Fernando Po with official collusion; President King resigned in 12/1930. {{gha-vii-ch28}}

blocks.q: A summary says African nationalism began with Manchester in 1945. Which evidence shows it is older?
o: The NCBWA (1920), Egypt's 1919 revolution and the Kikuyu Central Association (1924)

blocks.q: Egypt became 'independent' in 1922. Why should you qualify that?
o: Britain kept four reserved points, including defence and Sudan, and the 1936 treaty legalised the occupation

i: Nationalism grew inside Africa from about 1918, in elites and in rural protest. {{gha-vii-ch22}}
The NCBWA was co-operationist; Egypt's revolution won a qualified independence.
The 1935 invasion of Ethiopia joined Africa and the diaspora in protest.

blocks.x: Negritude
In 1930s Paris, Aime Cesaire of Martinique, Leopold Senghor of Senegal and Leon Damas of French Guiana developed Negritude. It affirmed African values against colonial assimilation. {{lib}}
Frantz Fanon, from Martinique and active in Algeria, later criticised its limits [CONTESTED]. {{lib}} Negritude lost its hold as the circumstances that produced it disappeared. {{gha-vii-ch21}}
The road to Manchester

Italy's invasion of Ethiopia stirred the diaspora. The International African Service Bureau followed in 1937, and Ras Makonnen's Manchester businesses gave future leaders a meeting place. {{gha-viii-ch23}}
The Pan-African Federation, formed in 1944 by Padmore, Kenyatta, Peter Abrahams, Wallace-Johnson and James, with Nkrumah joining later, organised the congress of 1945. {{gha-viii-ch23}}
Manchester, October 1945
The Fifth Pan-African Congress was organised by George Padmore and Kwame Nkrumah with Du Bois as honorary chair. Jomo Kenyatta, Peter Abrahams and Hastings Banda also took part. {{lib}}

It was the first Congress with a majority of African delegates, and it called for complete independence and for strikes and boycotts. No Africans from French, Portuguese or Belgian territories attended. {{gha-viii-ch05}}
One survey calls Manchester the sixth Pan-African Congress. {{rd-mau}} It is conventionally the fifth, as the UNESCO history also calls it. {{gha-viii-ch24}}
Accra, 1958
After Ghana's independence, the Conference of Independent African States met in April 1958 and the All-African Peoples' Conference in December 1958. Nkrumah argued for political union. {{lib}}

blocks.title: Worked example: why Manchester was a turning point
steps: Ask who attended: a majority of African delegates, including future leaders such as Nkrumah, Kenyatta and Banda.
Ask what was demanded: complete independence, not reform, with strikes and boycotts as methods.
Ask who was missing: delegates from French, Portuguese and Belgian territories, so it was an anglophone turning point.
Verdict: it moved Pan-Africanism from diaspora advocacy to an African independence movement. 'Turning point' is a judgement, not a measurement [CONTESTED]. {{gha-viii-ch05}}

blocks.q: You are explaining why historians treat Manchester 1945 as a turning point. What made it different, and what is its limit?
o: A majority of African delegates demanding independence; but no delegates from French, Portuguese or Belgian territories
blocks.w: Name both the change and the gap. {{gha-viii-ch05}}

blocks.q: A student calls Negritude a political party. What is the correction?
o: It was a cultural and literary movement affirming African values against assimilation
blocks.w: Cesaire, Senghor and Damas developed it as a cultural movement. {{lib}}

i: Manchester 1945 demanded independence with a majority of African delegates. {{gha-viii-ch05}}
Negritude was a cultural movement; Fanon later criticised its limits [CONTESTED].
Accra 1958 put union on the agenda.

blocks.x: Two camps

By 1961 the Casablanca group, including Ghana, Guinea, Mali, Egypt and Morocco, favoured quick union. The Monrovia group, including Nigeria, Liberia, Senegal and Ethiopia, favoured cooperation among sovereign states. {{lib}}

Nkrumah's Africa Must Unite (1963) argued for a continental government. Julius Nyerere and others preferred gradual regional steps. {{lib}} The radical Casablanca school distrusted regional steps, while the moderate Monrovia school accepted them. {{gha-viii-ch14}}
The founding

Thirty states were represented at the conference that opened on 23/05/1963 and signed the Charter on 25/05/1963. Togo was not admitted after the assassination of President Olympio, and Morocco refused the invitation; both signed later. {{gha-viii-ch24}}
Thirty plus those two gives 32 (our arithmetic). One encyclopaedia summary gives 33 signatory governments, so say 'about 32 or 33' and name the source. {{wiki-oau}}

Even good secondary sources slip. The 2024 UNESCO volume calls the Sirte Declaration of 09/09/1999 the founding act of the OAU. {{gha-ix}} The OAU Charter was signed on 25/05/1963; Sirte launched the process that created the African Union. {{oau-charter}}
What the Charter says

Article III lists seven principles: sovereign equality, non-interference in internal affairs, respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of each state, peaceful settlement of disputes, condemnation of political assassination and of subversion by neighbouring states, dedication to the emancipation of dependent territories, and non-alignment. {{oau-charter}}

The preamble promises to fight neocolonialism in all its forms. The Charter names four principal institutions (Assembly, Council of Ministers, General Secretariat and a Commission of Mediation, Conciliation and Arbitration) and caps any member's budget share at 20 per cent. {{oau-charter}}

The Charter itself does not say 'existing borders'; it speaks of each state's territorial integrity. {{oau-charter}} The pledge to respect colonial-era borders, the uti possidetis principle, came from the Cairo resolution of 1964 [FIRM]. {{lib}}
Liberation and diplomacy

The OAU set up an African Liberation Committee of nine states based in Dar es Salaam, with a Special Fund from voluntary contributions, and declared 25 May African Liberation Day. {{gha-viii-ch24}} The Committee is not in the Charter text, so it came from a later resolution. {{oau-charter}}

Its diplomatic wins included non-recognition of Ian Smith's UDI, a UN Commission for Namibia and the Lusaka Manifesto of 14 to 16/04/1969. Its recognition decided which liberation movements counted. {{gha-viii-ch25}}

1963 to 1973 can be read as years of organisation and manifestos without concrete results, and 1973 to 1980 as the fruitful decade. That is a judgement, not a measurement. {{gha-viii-ch25}} [CONTESTED]
After the 1967 war only Guinea broke with Israel, but in 10/1973 seventeen sub-Saharan states did so. The first Arab-African summit met in Cairo from 7 to 9 March 1977. {{gha-viii-ch28}}

Critics call the OAU a club of presidents that failed to confront abusive governments. Supporters credit it with helping end white-minority rule and keeping most border wars limited [CONTESTED]. {{lib}}

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a charter against its context
steps: The non-interference clause answers the Congo crisis, which Module 4 covers, and fear of border change.
Read the text, then ask what problem it was written to solve.
A rule drafted to protect new states from outside meddling later protected abusive rulers from regional criticism (our reading).
Forty years on, the African Union changed the principle, which Module 7 covers.

blocks.q: In 1963 Casablanca wanted a strong union and Monrovia a looser one. Looking at the OAU's rules, which group did it resemble more?
o: Monrovia, with sovereign equality, non-interference and no supranational authority
Neither: it had a world army
blocks.w: The compromise was closer to Monrovia. {{oau-charter}}

blocks.q: An essay says 'the OAU Charter of 1963 froze the colonial borders'. What is the precise correction?
o: The Charter speaks of territorial integrity; the explicit pledge to keep colonial-era borders came in the Cairo resolution of 1964
blocks.w: Check the text before quoting it. {{oau-charter}}

i: The OAU compromised: sovereignty over union. {{oau-charter}}
Signatory counts differ (32 or 33) between sources.
The border pledge is from 1964, not the Charter; non-interference later shielded abusive rulers [CONTESTED].

lessons.title: Reading a famous fake: the Willie Lynch letter

blocks.x: Some documents become part of memory without being documents at all. The 'Willie Lynch letter' claims to be a speech given in 1712 by a slave owner named William or Willie Lynch to slaveholders on the James River in Virginia, explaining how to keep enslaved people divided and controlled. It is a modern hoax, not an authentic document, and it must not be used as evidence of what any slaveholder said or did. {{cobb}} {{sun}} {{longreads}}

Do not treat anything in the letter as a historical quotation or attribute it to a real eighteenth-century person. This lesson studies the document as a case of source criticism and names no 'quotes' from it beyond tiny labels.
Where it came from

The speech was first 'discovered' in 1970 and began its online life in 1993, when a reference librarian at a University of Missouri library uploaded it. One source names Kansas City and another St. Louis, so the sources disagree on the campus. {{longreads}} {{sun}}

A reporter traced a ten-page pamphlet to a distributor who said the closest he got to a source was a group called the Black Liberation Library, which published it in 1970. That group could not be traced further, and the St. Louis newspaper that first printed it had no provenance to offer. {{sun}}
The speech became widely known after Louis Farrakhan quoted from it at the Million Man March in October 1995. {{sun}}
Four tests of authenticity

blocks.title: Testing the letter
head: Test
What you ask
What the sources report
rows: Where did it come from, and who held it before it was printed?
No eighteenth-century manuscript, archive or reference; first printed about 1970 by a group that cannot be traced {{cobb}} {{sun}}
Could someone in 1712 have written these words?
'Program' (1837), 'indoctrination' (1832), 'self-refueling' (1811), 'outline' in its modern sense (1759), and a capital-B 'Black' {{cobb}}
Does it fit the world it describes?
Most West Indian planters were absentees, and one letter could not explain slave policy across many regions, crops and laws {{cobb}}
Does any independent source mention it or its author?
Historians consulted had never met the name in their research {{sun}}

blocks.x: The word 'lynching' has its own history. There is no reference to the term before 1768, 'Lynch law' came from mob violence against Tories after the American Revolution, and only in the 1880s did lynching become associated with Black victims. {{cobb}}

blocks.title: Worked example: a date test you can run (our arithmetic)
steps: The letter claims 1712. The first reference to 'lynching' is no earlier than 1768, and 'program' in its modern sense dates from 1837.
1768 minus 1712 is 56 years; 1837 minus 1712 is 125 years.
A text of 1712 cannot use words that appear 56 or 125 years later in those senses. Several such words together, not one, make the case.
Verdict: the text fails the language test, and it also fails the provenance test. {{cobb}} {{wiki-lynch}}

blocks.x: Why such documents spread

The letter bypassed the historians and went straight into popular argument, where it became a verbal footnote explaining what is wrong with Black people. That misreads slavery, and unity is not the same as unanimity. {{cobb}}
It seemed to answer how a small number of whites could control many. The historian Gerald Horne called it urban folklore that reduces a complicated history to a simple narrative. {{sun}}
It has travelled from rap lyrics to a 2007 film, but a fake's emotional power does not make it history. {{longreads}}
What real records look like

Real documents exist. A tract, Religious Instruction of the Negroes (Charles C. Jones, Savannah, 1842), by a proslavery Presbyterian minister, records that the statutes of the slave states forbade teaching enslaved people to read, and that owners could forbid religious meetings on their land. Jones's account is his own, not neutral history. {{cobb}} {{jones}}

British slavers mixed people of different African ethnicities on ships to make communication, and so rebellion, harder. {{cobb}} Many books and articles on slave management survive, so it is hard to see why anyone would invent a document. {{sun}}

The trade itself is documented in thousands of voyage records: the Slave Voyages estimates table gives 12,521,354 people embarked between 1501 and 1866, as Pre-Colonial Africa Module 8 showed. {{sv-est}}

Records of racial terror after slavery are also real and dated. A compilation of American newspaper reports on lynchings from 1880 to 1960 gives a newspaper, a place and a date for each item, and often a contradicting report. {{gz-press}}

blocks.title: Real counts differ, but each has a named source
head: Source
Figure
Note
rows: Defined by legal evidence of a death, illegality, three or more participants {{gz-tuskegee}}

blocks.x: A real forced-labour system built after emancipation, convict leasing, is documented from court, company and federal records: by 1877 every former Confederate state except Virginia leased convicts. {{bm-origins}} A real system leaves records that can be checked; the Willie Lynch letter has no document behind it.
Take a quotation you have seen online. Run the four tests on it and write one line for each: provenance, language, internal logic, corroboration.

blocks.q: A friend shares a quotation from a '1712 speech' that uses the word 'program'. Which test does it fail, and why?
o: Language and anachronism: 'program' did not carry its modern meaning until 1837
blocks.w: A word can date a text. {{cobb}}

blocks.q: Someone says 'the letter is not real, but it is true in spirit'. Why is that risky?
o: It treats a fake as evidence and hides the real, documented sources
It means the letter is authentic
blocks.w: Real evidence is plentiful, and fiction cannot substitute for fact. {{sun}}

i: The Willie Lynch letter is a modern hoax: no provenance, anachronistic language, doubtful logic, no corroboration. {{cobb}} {{sun}} {{longreads}}
Test any document on provenance, language, logic and corroboration.
Real records of slavery and racial terror exist, with names and dates. {{sv-est}} {{gz-press}}
